newsitem.title: INDIA: Death toll from India cyclone may reach 2,000.
newsitem.headline: Death toll from India cyclone may reach 2,000.

text.p: A cyclone that swept through low-lying coastland of southeast India last week may have killed 2,000 people, officials said on Monday as rescuers searched for fishermen who put to sea before the storm hit.
The air and sea search continued for around 1,000 fishermen who were working off the Andhra Pradesh coast where the cyclone hit shore on Wednesday, destroying houses, livestock and crops.
But hopes were fading as hundreds of bodies had already been washed ashore, according to local reports.

"There is a flickering hope that they will be found," said an official in Amalapuram, close to the stretch of coast that took the full blast of the 180 kmp (110 mph) winds and three metre (10 foot) tidal waves.
Local fishing leaders disputed official statements that cyclone warnings were issued 24 hours ahead of the storm.

"The number 10 warning, indicating a severe cyclone, was sounded only hours before the storm hit the coast, by which time the fishermen had already been out at sea," said one of the leaders, Malladi Swamy.
Officials said some villages in the Amalapuram area, where an estimated 100,000 people lived, were still inaccessible.
But Andhra Pradesh government spokesman B.P. Acharaya said the overall death toll would not rise above 2,000. "It will be around 2,000 maximum," he told Reuters.
The government of the southeast state has called on New Delhi to release more relief funds.

It also sought help from international agencies through a message broadcast on the Internet to cope with the calamity that will cost an estimated 53.75 billion rupees ($1.5 billion) in damage to crops and property.
"The people of Andhra Pradesh look forward to you for support and assistance in overcoming this calamity," it said.
"The extent and severity of damage caused by the cyclone certainly qualifies to be treated as not only a national calamity but a grave human tragedy," it said.
A relief official said: "No response has so far been received but we are hopeful that aid will certainly come."

Survivors in the two prosperous coastal districts of east and west Godavari have complained that help has not come fast enough while officials in the state capital Hyderabad said relief and rescue workers were on a war-footing.
The officials said efforts were under way to prevent epidemics of waterborne diseases like cholera.
"Inoculation of a large number of people is on and well water is being chlorinated," state health minister Metla Satyanarayana said.
The stench of putrifying flesh from the bloated carcasses of dead cattle floating in the canals that criss-cross the Godavari river delta region filled the air close to camps and villages.
Dr Vijay Kumar at the Relief Control Room in Hyderabad said there had been no confirmed diseases reported but that the picture would become clearer in a few days.
"With drinking water cut off and existing supplies contaminated it is quite possible but there are no confirmed reports of any cases so far," Kumar told Reuters.
There were close to 200,000 people huddled in the makeshift relief camps and more than 400 medical teams treating the sick and injured, officials said.
One of those seeking aid was Para Durga, a middle-aged woman with shrunken cheeks, who stood in line with a few ragged bundles of belongings.
"We have hardly eaten anything," she said.
